My two cents is that it's just a worthless quote.

I've been using Neovim for very nearly as long as it has been around, and I find the project to be a pleasure to use. My editor experience is better now than it ever was on Vim, and it is due to a lot of hard work and effort on the part of a lot of people who have made this project a success.

"Full-screen Neovim looks cool as hell" genuinely doesn't make sense as praise to me, as someone who has used Neovim in a full screen terminal window for more than a decade. What Neovim looks like is unique to each user, and that is fundamental to the promise of Neovim. The only value of the quote can possibly be DHH's name, and that is at least as much a liability as a boon.

My initial reaction to this was that I'd still continue to use Neovim, and I'm not going to make threats to go use something else, because that's just a naive and childish thing to threaten. This reaction dims Neovim's brand from my perspective, and I think that's a shame.

> Neovim is the last piece of software we need drama in ATM.

There are always new attempts at creating drama. Previously it was use of GitHub itself (twice), then reddit, then X/twitter, then AI, and many other cases before that.

I'm not going to defend any particular thing and I'm not going to react to your demands.

You cannot pretend open source and public relations are not intertwined. I've been doing this work for a decade - yes, they are. Quiet lurker and community member here; been a neovim user for the last few years.

I think it might be worth asking what the goal of the quote is, and what its impact is.

Does it expand the community, or does it jeopardize its stability?

Does it provide meaningful social proof that's otherwise needed?

What does the presence of a quote from someone advocating for ethnic cleansing indicate to new and existing users about the project and its leadership?

Whether the quote is removed or not, I advocate careful consideration it from the angle of community stewardship. We all do a bunch of calculations when evaluating software we adopt. The health of the community and its leadership can be an outsized part of those calculations when the software benefits from such a robust extension ecosystem. 

When the quote remains — which demonstrates at best indifference to, and at worst, endorsement of a future where some members of the community are not welcome because of who they are — its conspicuous presence is a message. How many plugin developers, potential future core contributors, or neovim evangelists might find themselves reflected in this list and feel unwelcome? What direction does that indicate for the community? 

When you're likely to sink hours into customization into a program, it's reasonable to be concerned or to hesitate if a non-trivial part of the community had misgivings.

And if that's (edit: _not_) enough, conversely, apart from the disappointment of those who appreciate those beliefs, what problems would its removal cause?

I've got a question out of genuine curiosity: 

Would the response be different if this issue was instead a PR with the quote removed and a polite explanation, without including the `Do what you want with this information.` line?

Community management takes time, that's just the kind of website neovim currently has.

> Would the response be different if this issue was instead a PR with the quote removed and a polite explanation, without including the Do what you want with this information. line?

Maybe! The only reason I made an issue in the first place is because I love the editor, which is deeply integrated into my workflow. That is to say, I care enough about its success to say something.

The remark was more about my sentiment to try to keep using this thing than it was about leaning in hard like a jerk. What I did not expect was an inflamed, defensive response to information about a trivial, whimsical one-liner on a website. Because make no mistake, the quote is trivial. Trivial to acknowledge, trivial to remove and also trivial to distance yourself from by simply agreeing not to endorse DHH's views. What isn't as trivial is "fighting back" against the feedback.

On that note, that's really what boggles my mind about all of this.
@justinmk : You have gone from a project which doesn't drive away anyone in particular to one that does, for literally no reason beyond "well I don't feel like the guy was that bad so i'm not removing the quote"/"I don't think people should be able to force projects into opinions!"/whatever. When the reality is you're literally forcing your political opinions onto everyone working on this project by making them choose between working on technology and aligning themselves with someone a lot of us are deeply uncomfortable with who doesn't even contribute to the project. I'm sorry to @ you like this but as someone who's been using this editor for years, maintains a neovim client, and actively attempts to contribute back to this project whenever I can - please take the responsibility of this more seriously.

Not speaking on behalf of the X.org foundation, but speaking from my experience here: we literally regularly get some of the most talented contributors I have seen from any community, and a huge portion of them would want nothing to do with X or freedesktop if we didn't take action on things like this. I know because I've spoken to them, I've even spoken to a number of them who specifically don't want anything to do with any other portions of the Linux community entirely because someone on the other end convinced themselves "people issues aren't my problem/people issues just waste my time". seriously. This entire project, any open source project for this matter, is a people issue. And I know it is the action we take that does this because I have watched many people leave kernel development, stay on mesa development, and explicitly state this as one of the reasons for doing so. Some of these people are responsible for enormous portions of drivers like panfrost, NVK, nouveau, radv, you name it.

Consider the motivations you're now changing for someone to join this project as well. Previously, the main reason for someone contributing to this project would be because they use this text editor and want to give back. Now you have a potential onslaught of 'contributors' whose entire desire for being involved with this project is not because they have skills, or talent, but because they saw neovim "got cancelled" or whatever. On the other hand, if neovim just literally removes the quote and stops engaging you are, again, pushing away no one in particular. There will likely be echoes of this thread on social media for a while, but it does literally go away if you just do damage control.

See: https://world.hey.com/dhh/as-i-remember-london-e7d38e64

To quote:

> That was then. Now, I wouldn't dream of it. London is no longer the city I was infatuated with in the late '90s and early 2000s. Chiefly because it's [no longer full of native Brits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_groups_in_London). In 2000, more than sixty percent of the city were native Brits. By 2024, that had dropped to about a third. A statistic as evident as day when you walk the streets of London now.

He quotes a Wikipedia page there, and it's enlightening to look at what that page in detail. He says that "more than sixty percent of the city were native Brits. By 2024, that had dropped to about a third." The data that lines up with this stated progression is the census data for "White: British." Not any other type white ethnic group, nor any other type of native-born British person, just white British. If we scroll through the same Wikipedia page, and try and give him the benefit of the doubt, the 2011 number for foreign-born Londoners does not match what he's claiming. If you think "oh, maybe he looked at the census data and didn't link it," [here's the census data](https://apps.london.gov.uk/census-2021-reports/#/country-of-birth), and it doesn't support what he's saying. I can't imagine it was an accident, since the language of the Wikipedia table was obvious.

He's clearly talking about the number of white people vs non-white people, that's the only way his statement makes sense. And of course it makes sense, since if one were to think about it a moment, it'd be obvious that it's impossible to know the country of birth of someone (or their legal status) just from looking at them. This is all an aside that he's talking so positively about Tommy Robinson's march, which should speak for itself.

This is to say, that it goes beyond his views of "remigration," but who he deems as worthy of belonging in Europe (he also extrapolates this to Copenhaguen), and from his own words and citations, it's just white people.
